utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, my request would be if we could take the break now, and I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I would appreciate that. I don't know who's doing the cross-examination, but this should be completed within the time left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't know either. We're just waiting to see what happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I do not have - and I haven't checked with Judges Janu and Taya - I don't have the summary of the next two witnesses. Neither this one who is coming now after the break --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour will find, like we found, that Mr. Cunningham put -- although it only said one summary when it was e-mailed, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I attached all three.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You attached all three. That's what I mean, yes. The title just said summary for the first witness but all three were --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll get you copies during the break. I didn't give you any exhibits either because, after proofing this witness last night, there were really no exhibits that I could use with her.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just mention -- I don't know whether we're in closed session or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's all right if we're open, simply to say that the indictment should be signed by the Prosecutor today. We had to wait until she returned, and it will be filed, we hope, this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, Ms. Korner. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome. You are about to start giving evidence in this case which has been going on against Radoslav Brdjanin, and our Rules require that before you do so, you make a solemn declaration to us that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Usher is going to hand you the text of this solemn declaration. Please read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat. You have met Mr. Cunningham already. Mr. Cunningham, as Defence counsel for Mr. Brdjanin, will be asking you a few questions. He will then be followed by Ms. Sutherland from the Prosecution. And we hope to finish with you today so that you can go back to your family and to your country. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your name is Radosava Dzombic, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Dzombic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I knew I wouldn't get it right. Thank you for correcting me. What municipality were you born in?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I was born in Bosanska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In which municipality do you currently live?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I live in the Municipality of Celinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how long have you lived in Celinac?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Approximately 35 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You are a Serb by ethnicity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And are you married?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Are you currently working?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where do you work at?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I work in the municipality as the secretary of the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How long have you worked for the Municipality of Celinac?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I've been working close to 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And how long have you worked as a secretary for the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Well, almost as long.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I want to take you back to the early 1990s before the multiparty elections. Before the multiparty elections, did you know an individual by the name of Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him by sight, Radoslav Brdjanin. Radoslav Brdjanin, I knew him by sight before he came to work with us. I knew he was a construction engineer. I knew that he was working in a construction company called 25 November.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether or not before he started working at the municipality, whether Mr. Brdjanin was considered competent as an engineer?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was quite highly regarded as an engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How is it that Mr. Brdjanin -- how is it that you became Mr. Brdjanin's secretary?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I was working at that post prior to his arrival, and that is how I remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What position did Mr. Brdjanin assume within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: He worked as the president of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you know in rough terms when he assumed the position as President of the Executive Board of Celinac? Do you know what year that would have been?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: He was appointed in 1991, but I think that he came from the assembly in December 1990, a few days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What was his -- what were his duties as president of the Executive Board of Celinac, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: The -- through the executive board, everything was being resolved. There were other members. All the problems were being resolved concerning the municipality. He had also days of open, public hours where people would come to resolve certain problems or other issues. So he had meetings with people from the economy. So it was the executive board of the assembly. And everything passes through this body, and it is here that solutions are found.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll come back to some of the things that you mentioned in that answer. Let's go back to the time when Mr. Brdjanin first took office. At that time when he took office, were there professionals with experience in municipal government working there in Celinac?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were these professionals members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know whether, when Mr. Brdjanin took office, there was any pressure to replace these non-SDS professionals within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Do you mean by Mr. Brdjanin or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I mean pressure being placed on Mr. Brdjanin, whether there was pressure on him to do something about these --

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Pressure on Mr. Brdjanin, yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Were you a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No, no, I have not been.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When Mr. Brdjanin took office, did he replace the professionals within the municipal government with SDS members?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you know why he kept the professionals?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: He kept them because they worked in a correct manner and professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did any of the people that he kept, were any of them non-Serbs or members of mixed marriages? Let's break that down, that's not a fair question. Were any of the people that he kept working in the municipality, were any of those people non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. The head of the accountancy department, the driver, as well as the registrar, the marriage registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were any of the people he kept working for him after the elections, were any of them parties to a mixed marriage?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No, these were Muslims who were married to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you work with Mr. Brdjanin on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And as a result of that, did you have the opportunity to see the sort of work habits that he had?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How would you describe those habits for the Court?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Brdjanin was a hard-working person. He also demanded of others to do good work, quality work, and to do it on time. And he was like that himself also.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. You told us earlier that Mr. Brdjanin, as part of his duties, would see citizens that had problems. Did that happen -- how often did that happen during the week?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: One day in the week was set aside for open office hours for the public and for all issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. In 1991, 1992, what was the majority people in Celinac?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: The majority people were the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you this in a leading fashion, hoping not to draw an objection, but would you agree with me that the vast majority of the population in Celinac was Serbian?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, getting back to these meetings that Mr. Brdjanin had on a weekly basis, who would come to him with problems? Would there be Serbs and non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Everybody would come, whoever had a problem or needed to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And would that group include the non-Serbian population of Celinac?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to see Mr. Brdjanin as he conducted these meetings with the non-Serbian population who came to him with their problems?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would pass through my office. I'd announce their arrival. Sometimes I knew why they were coming; sometimes I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how would Mr. Brdjanin treat the non-Serbian population who came to his office in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Well, his attitude was the same to everyone regardless, irrespective of who was coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how would you describe that attitude?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Well, he attempted to listen and hear what the problems of the people were, and to the best of his abilities he tried to resolve them and to help at the times as they were. They were all represented, and he looked upon all of them in the same fashion, all of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In the time that you worked with Mr. Brdjanin, did you ever see him act improperly or incorrectly with regards to the non-Serbs who came to visit him in his office?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him express -- Mr. Brdjanin ever express any hatred, animosity, dislike towards the non-Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: In -- when I was present, I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You mentioned this earlier, that one of the Muslim employees within the municipality was his driver. Do you remember that individual's name?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes; Nezirovic Hilmija.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: During the time that you were working with Mr. Brdjanin, did you ever have the opportunity to observe the relationship between the driver and Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was that relation like?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nezirovic was always close by, at hand, for Mr. Brdjanin, and they had quite a correct relationship and a good relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was -- did you ever see Mr. Brdjanin act inappropriately or incorrectly with respect to the driver?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to take you to 1992, and did there come a time in Celinac where there was some explosions and destruction of property within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: On the territory of the municipality, yes, occasionally there were some such situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, does the municipality of Kotor Varos, is that a municipality that borders the municipality of Celinac?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you become aware of clashes in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware of a Bosniak, a Muslim citizen approaching Mr. Brdjanin for help with respect to those clashes in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that man. The name is Talic, Meho. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Talic was the one who approached Mr. Brdjanin. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what -- did he have a problem that he wanted Mr. Brdjanin's assistance with?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: He had a daughter who at the time was working in Kotor Varos. She was working as a waitress. And these activities began in Kotor Varos. He became afraid for his daughter, and he contacted Mr. Brdjanin, asking him to go there to find that daughter, to locate that daughter of his, and to see how she is doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Brdjanin's response to a Muslim citizen who wanted his assistance with respect to his daughter? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: He asked our head for civilian defence to go there with the man. He also gave them the municipal vehicle, and to go there in order to find that daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not that trip to Kotor Varos was a dangerous trip?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was dangerous. Our chief couldn't pass that checkpoint. They only allowed Meho to pass, and our man, the municipal director, remained there. He wasn't allowed to cross the checkpoint, the border there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: By using Mr. Brdjanin's car with his permission, were they able to retrieve Mr. Talic's daughter from Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Talic was able to get in touch with the daughter. I'm not sure if he brought her back, but everything was all right. He spent some time with her there, and probably left her somewhere safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And what was Mr. Talic's reaction to Mr. Brdjanin's assistance?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: He was certainly very happy that he was given an opportunity to get in touch with his daughter, to see her. And he was grateful to Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did Mr. Brdjanin have any hesitation in helping this individual, this Bosniak individual who needed assistance?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about another situation and see if you can assist the Court in this. What is the -- is Celinac an urban municipality, that is, a municipality with cities, or is it largely a rural municipality with small towns?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: The municipality itself is a small one. It has plenty of local communes and villages around them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And is there some farming, some agricultural work within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly around the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. In 1992, was there a concern about bringing in the harvest, the spring harvest?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. The conditions were as they were at the time. There was a great deal of concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did Mr. Brdjanin do anything to help the Muslim farmers bring in their harvest during this time period?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: He secured combines which first went to the Muslim villages because they're at the far end of our municipality. They started there, and then made the rounds of all the other villages to help bring in the harvest.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was there any hesitation on his part in assisting the Muslim farmers bring in their harvests in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No hesitation, no. It was necessary to bring in the harvest and put it away safely as soon as possible. As I said, Mr. Brdjanin was a fair man, and he treated all people fairly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, in the spring of 1992, was there an incident in the Municipality of Celinac involving threats made to the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: There were a number of -- well, I mean, those things were done by certain individuals. I don't know. I know that things did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Well, and that was a bad question on my part. You worked in the municipal building. One day at work, did you become aware of a large segment of the Muslim population of Celinac gathered outside the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know why those Muslims had gathered in front of the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Well, they were afraid of what started happening, and they wanted to leave Celinac. Mostly those were women, children, and elderly men who wanted to leave. They were afraid of shootouts across town. There was a lot of random shooting. There was no intent to kill anyone in particular, but there was a lot of shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Everyone was scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether -- well, let me ask this question: Did Mr. Brdjanin do anything to protect the Muslim population that had gathered in front of the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that those people had to be put in a building, which was the elementary school in town, and that food and drinks should be given for them and that they would see if they could get a vehicle for them to leave town because they insisted on leaving town.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, were these individuals who were placed in the elementary school, these Muslims, were they protected?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Security was provided. Mr. Brdjanin got in touch with the police and requested that security be provided for the night they stayed there, and the day. He insisted on them being safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Were these people being detained? Were they locked up, or how would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No, they were just put up there in order to avoid them standing outside the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Why -- do you know why they -- I'm sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Because they did not want to return home. They insisted on leaving Celinac. I'm not sure where it was they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And did Mr. Brdjanin to you seem to be concerned for the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. He didn't know what to do with them. The conditions that were there at the time, there was no fuel. There was no one to take them away by bus. This couldn't be dealt with quickly, this sort of problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know whether the -- and if I've asked this, I apologise. Do you know whether the Muslim population that was kept inside the school, whether they were allowed to leave, to go to their homes if they needed to?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what happened to this group of Muslims after -- Did they ultimately leave the school?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: A number of them certainly left. I'm not sure about the figures. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I'm sure you understand. Once transport was provided, they did leave. I'm not sure where they left for, but probably it was a destination of their own choosing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Did any of the Muslim population stay in Celinac during this period, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did any of those Muslims who stayed in Celinac and had been put up in the school, did any of them ever come to the municipality to express their gratitude to Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes. Some were put up at the school, and those who stayed were those who never wanted to leave, those who went to the army later on and those who still lived there, those who were in touch with Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Brdjanin leaving his position as president of the executive board?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I do remember the time he left, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And after he left, did he attend -- do you remember him attending meetings of the assembly or the Crisis Staff of Celinac Municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin and I were no longer in touch following his departure. Therefore, I can't remember whether he came back or not. If he did come back, this was certainly not taking place at the municipal building. I never saw him again later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cunningham. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Dzombic, when Mr. Brdjanin was dealing with the collection of Muslims which were outside of the municipal assembly building, he was still working with the executive board?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier the Muslim harvest. Was there a shortage of food and other supplies in the Celinac Municipality at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So the Muslim harvest would have gone to all of the population within the Celinac Municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where would the harvest have gone?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Where I come from, farmers are into production, and the areas are very small. Everyone produces as much as they can for themselves, for their own needs, and the harvest was meant for whoever had sown it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned a person called Meho Talic who Mr. Brdjanin assisted. Is that person called Mehmed Talic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps Mehmed, yes. I know him as Meho. I think his name is Mehmed and Meho is a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: He's not a friend of mine, but he is an acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I've known him as a client at work or as a man I tend to meet in the street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was how long have you known him in either of these two or both of these two capacities. How long? Five years? Ten years? Twenty years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've known him since I arrived in Celinac. Celinac is a small town. You know almost everyone there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who did you report to when you worked at the municipal assembly building?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Who did I report to? Well, Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, I'll be more precise. In 1992 --

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: In 1992, Mr. Brdjanin. But there was the municipal secretary, too, who was another person I worked with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: At that time, back in 1992, I believe it was Andjelko Topic at the time. But please don't take my word for it. I'm not sure I can remember after all these years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As secretary, did you report to the head of the joint technical services department?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you take the minutes at the municipal assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did anyone else take minutes?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Depending on the time. If I had other business to take care of, there was another lady who did the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was that Maricka Vojatovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, Maricka Vojatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know where she currently resides today?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: She resides in Celinac, but she also owns a flat in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're aware that a crisis staff was set up in Celinac, are you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I am aware of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. Brdjanin was a member of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: He may have been, but I had nothing to do with the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who took the minutes of the crisis staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. It may have been one of them or someone else. I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you mean "one of them," you mean a member of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I am referring to members of the crisis staff. It may have been one of the members.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Dzombic, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you type any documents relating to the Celinac crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where are the minutes of the municipal assembly kept?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: At the municipal assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're still working there today?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So in exactly which room are they housed, are they archived?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Some of the documents are probably in the archive, and some are still with the secretary of the president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Which documents would the secretary of the municipal assembly keep in his own possession?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: All the materials adopted at an assembly session are deposited in the archive, in the files. Or rather, some of them are deposited in the files and the more recent ones are kept in the secretary's cupboard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So all the ones from 1992 would be housed where you said they were?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where would the minutes from the crisis staff meetings be archived?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Probably in the archive, the archive that is inside the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Have you ever been asked to obtain any minutes of the Celinac Crisis Staff meetings, or retrieve?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No. I only took the minutes at meetings of the executive board, and that's the only thing I kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: My question was have you ever been asked by any person to retrieve any minutes of the Celinac Crisis Staff meetings since 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No. No one ever asked me any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There would be no reason to hide or destroy crisis staff minutes, would there?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No, there wouldn't. But I have nothing to do with that. I didn't take the minutes, I didn't attend the meetings. I was doing my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any of Mr. Brdjanin's public speeches?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No. We had no electricity, even for 40 days at a time. Sometimes we had electricity for two hours only, and I didn't know whether to switch on a vacuum cleaner or the water heater to have a bath. I really couldn't give a toss about politics. I had my family and my children to look after. I didn't read the papers. We didn't feel like following any of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In 1991 and early 1992, did you ever hear any of Mr. Brdjanin's public speeches?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I wasn't into that. I wasn't into politics then or now. I'm simply not interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever watch television?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Well, I did, but I told you about the power cuts that would last for 40 days at a time. It is very difficult for me to sit down in front of a TV and watch TV because I was just too busy for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you have power cuts in 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: 1992, yes, there were power cuts. In 1993 early, and later on in May, my mother took ill again, and I took her to Serbia for treatment. So Maricka Vojatovic stood in for me throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you have power cuts in early 1992? Prior to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: How am I supposed to know? I know that there were power cuts and that there were problems with electricity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before the war broke out, were there power cuts in Celinac?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Even nowadays. The power lines are very old and rickety. It's just that the power cuts are not as long as they used to be in those years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In 1991, did you watch television?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: From time to time, from time to time. You do watch TV, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Brdjanin on television?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I may have heard of sessions or something sometimes, but I didn't watch anything else. If there was something I wanted to watch and if we had electricity, I would always watch something that was entertaining. I just wasn't into politics. I was never a member of any party or anything. Even today, I still don't really watch the news because I'm not interested. And this should be easy for you to verify.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever listen to the radio?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Radio. Music, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Brdjanin became president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Brdjanin describing Muslims as "non-Christian scum"?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just have one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Is there re-examination, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Janu, do you have any questions? Judge Janu from the Czech Republic would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Madam, those Muslim people who were leaving, were there any friends among them, friends of yours?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: No, no. No friends of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: You never had Muslim friends?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Only those who worked with me. Those were workmates. We would socialise at work, but no special friends in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And all those miraculously stayed in Celinac Municipality, those you worked with?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Well, they stayed. Mr. Nezirovic stayed until the law on administrative pensions was adopted, and then he retired alongside another three persons, men or women, who were Serbs. The rest of them left their jobs of their own free will and went abroad. I'm telling you about the people who worked in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: You said that there was a lot of shooting, but there was no intent to kill anybody. So how do you know there wasn't the intent to kill anybody?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Because no one was killed in Celinac. Those were no military operations, that wasn't a war. On the other hand, everyone had weapons, if you see my point. In the evening, we would all lock our doors and shut ourselves up in our homes. There would be shooting, but not a single person was killed. There was no case that someone was killed, not in the town itself at any rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So your explanation for yourself is that the Muslims were leaving; Serbs were not leaving. So what was your explanation, that Serbs were more courageous than the Muslims, or what explanation did you give yourself? You're a lady, you are married, you have children, and I know you said you were not interested in politics, but this wasn't only the politics; this was something very awkward was happening around you. So how did you view that situation?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Madam, who am I to say where other people should go or if they should stay? How on earth am I supposed to know why they wanted to leave? There was a lot of fear probably because they were, after all, the minority population in that town. That's the assumption, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So just the feeling that they belonged to the minority made them to leave, in your opinion. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you not to ask me these questions because these are political questions. The Serbs also in other towns and places were a minority, and they had to flee because they felt jeopardised. It was the same for both Serbs and Muslims. Those were the times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. I wasn't asking you any political questions; I was asking you only the questions about the life and the situation in which you stayed and participated as a worker of the municipality. So that's all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Taya, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: No, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I don't have any questions either.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May I ask a follow-up question from Judge Janu's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What would that be? Would you tell us what the question is first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to killings that occurred in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Dzombic, were you aware of the killings that occurred in the Celinac Municipality which were committed by the members of the Zigic [phoen] family on the 31st of July and the 1st of August in particular?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: Sugic is the name. That's at the far end of our municipality, the villages you're talking about where this happened. It was far away from where I lived, but yes, I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you hear that it was Muslims that were killed by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOSAVA DZOMBIC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mrs. Dzombic, that brings us to the end of your testimony. On behalf of the Tribunal, I should like to thank you for having come over to The Hague and to this Tribunal to give evidence in this trial against Radoslav Brdjanin. You will be escorted out of the courtroom by Mr. Usher, and you will be attended to to facilitate your return back home. On behalf of everyone present here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And she can leave the exhibits, and I'll pick it up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Leave that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose that's all for today, Mr. Cunningham. The next witness is not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Is not present and not ready yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I invite Your Honour and, through Mr. Cunningham, Mr. Ackerman to perhaps tomorrow, if there's time, which I anticipate there will be, we're obviously not going to be sitting Thursday now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's only one more witness and it's a relatively short witness, I believe. To perhaps, if Mr. Ackerman can attend so we can discuss, please, in advance which witnesses are coming now in January and February and proper summaries --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- in advance. We still haven't got a summary for Monday's witness, which is a major witness, other than the four-line saying we interviewed him and that will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That has been my task to get that done, but because I've done a good part of the last witnesses, I haven't done that yet. But this is also a witness that they have interviewed for several hours in Banja Luka. So it's not a total surprise. But I understand what our obligation is, and I will get that to you today. Mr. Ackerman will be here in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And based on the representations made by the Prosecutor last week that they thought this next witness -- we had allocated one day for him, and the Prosecution said it would probably be more than that, so based on that representation we factored that into our scheduling of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And do I take it that Witness Number 8, who would be the next witness after the next, will be coming on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: He will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to ask that as well, because as Your Honour will recall, I said I wanted a definite confirmation that the witness was coming who we'd interviewed, in which case once we've got that confirmation -- that is a definite, isn't it? We're not suddenly going to be told he's not coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When I checked last night, he's still coming. Mr. Ackerman and I will be here in the morning and we'll confirm it as best we can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But, Your Honour, I think for the reasons I keep on explaining, Your Honour, we would like to know now which of the remaining 35-odd witnesses is actually going to testify in the intervening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- 12th of January and 12th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll deal with that tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Just let me give the Chamber an idea of where we are at as a Defence. We are going to spend our first day where we don't have Court, sitting down with our witness list, going through, knowing exactly who is going to come. Our witness list is solid through the Christmas break, and it would be our guess -- my guess that we would have our final list ready probably by Friday afternoon. We are going to try to sit down and do it on Thursday when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thursday it seems we will not be sitting, from what I gather. And Friday, of course not, because we have got Plenary in the morning as well. So we will take it up from there tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of December, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.34 p.m.,
